customer_question: The RF tester's log shows Enhanced Power Control set to True, but the Test Plan's ICS says it should be No -- does this mismatch affect the test result, and do we need to retest?
question_variants: Why doesn't the tester's logged setting match the ICS in the Test Plan?
Is it OK to test with the ICS set to 'all supported' instead of the customer's officially declared ICS?
Does a setting mismatch on one feature affect other test items' results?
Do we need to redo this RF test because of the ICS discrepancy?
actual_issue: A reviewer found that the RF tester's log showed Enhanced Power Control configured as supported (True), while the Test Plan's ICS stated it should be unsupported (No) -- meaning the DUT configuration used during measurement did not match the ICS specification on file, raising the question of whether this affected the test result and whether a retest was needed.
plain_english_explanation: Sometimes the lab isn't fully confident about exactly which optional features a customer's product actually supports, so instead of guessing wrong and missing something, the tester is deliberately configured to assume every possible feature is supported, so every relevant test gets run. If the product turns out not to actually support a given feature, the test for that one feature reports accordingly, and that alone doesn't change the results of the other, unrelated tests. This explains why a setting in the test log might look like it doesn't match what was officially declared for the ICS.
consultant_answer: In RF testing, the test items executed correspond to the ICS entered into the tester; for any item the DUT does not actually support, the response indicates non-support, and this particular tester configuration choice has no effect on the results of other test items. It is true that the ICS on file and the tester's configured setting did not match in this instance, but given the tight test schedule, this was accepted rather than triggering a retest. The underlying practice: since the customer's actual ICS wasn't confidently known, the tester was deliberately configured with all items set to 'supported' so that every possible item would be tested as a precaution; the report was then issued by confirming that every item the product actually responded to as supported was a Pass.
decision_logic: Configuring the RF tester's ICS more broadly ('all supported') than the customer's officially declared ICS is an acceptable practice when the customer's actual ICS is not confidently known, because it ensures complete test coverage without risk: any item the DUT does not actually support is recorded accordingly, and that non-support does not affect the outcome of unrelated test items. A mismatch between the tester's configured setting and the on-file ICS, discovered after the fact, does not by itself require a retest if it can be confirmed the mismatched item's outcome did not affect other items' results.
final_recommendation: When the customer's officially declared ICS is uncertain, consider deliberately configuring the tester with a broader 'all supported' ICS so every possible item is exercised, and report based on which items the DUT actually responds to as supported. If a tester-configuration-vs.-ICS mismatch is discovered during report review, confirm it did not affect other test items' results before deciding whether a retest is warranted, weighing this against schedule constraints.
risk_if_done_wrong: Assuming a tester-configuration mismatch automatically invalidates the test or requires a full retest, without first checking whether it affected only the specific mismatched item, could trigger unnecessary retesting under schedule pressure; conversely, failing to verify that a mismatch didn't affect other items' results before accepting it risks an inaccurate report.
